_note: Per-station photo quest. `hook` is a fact about the place (flavor only, never an instruction). The task the player does comes from `questId` in data/photo-quests.json, and is always something any T station has. Keyed by UI slug (components/run/stations.ts).

alewife.hook: Alewife is named for a small herring that still swims up the Mystic River every spring.

davis.hook: Davis Square was a busy rail crossing long before it was a music hub.

porter.hook: The porterhouse steak may take its name from a hotel that once stood here.

harvard.hook: The statue in Harvard Yard is known as the "statue of three lies."

central.hook: Cambridge City Hall, steps away, was a philanthropist's gift in 1889.

kendall.hook: MIT moved across the river from Boston to Cambridge in 1916.

charles.hook: In 1846, surgeons nearby first demonstrated ether anesthesia in public.

park.hook: Park Street opened in 1897 as part of America's first subway tunnel.

downtown.hook: Washington Street once ran along the Neck, the only road into Boston.

south.hook: When it opened in 1899, South Station was among the busiest stations on Earth.

lechmere.hook: Lechmere is named for Richard Lechmere, a Loyalist whose land was seized in the Revolution.

science.hook: The Museum of Science sits on top of the old Charles River Dam.

north.hook: In 1919, a wave of molasses swept through nearby streets at about 35 mph.

haymarket.hook: Haymarket's open-air produce stalls have run here for nearly two centuries.

gov.hook: Scollay Square, once Boston's rowdiest district, was razed for City Hall Plaza.

boylston.hook: Boylston opened in 1897 and is one of the oldest subway stops in the Americas.

arlington.hook: The Public Garden's Swan Boats have been pedaled by foot since 1877.

copley.hook: Trinity Church rests on about 4,500 wooden pilings driven into filled marsh.

hynes.hook: Hynes is named for John B. Hynes, the mayor who led Boston through the 1950s.

kenmore.hook: The glowing sign over Kenmore Square has lit the skyline since 1965.

sullivan.hook: Sullivan Square is named for James Sullivan, governor of Massachusetts in 1807 and 1808.

ccollege.hook: The 1775 Battle of Bunker Hill was fought nearby, mostly on Breed's Hill.

state.hook: In 1776 the Declaration of Independence was read from the Old State House balcony above this station.

chinatown.hook: Chinatown's ornate gate, a gift from Taiwan, was dedicated in 1982.

backbay.hook: Back Bay really was a bay: its tidal flats were filled in during the 1800s.

ruggles.hook: In 1987 the Orange Line moved here, replacing the old elevated tracks above Washington Street.

foresthills.hook: The Arnold Arboretum, founded by Harvard in 1872, is right next door.

blandford.hook: Here the B branch comes up out of the tunnel and onto Commonwealth Avenue.

bueast.hook: From the 1910s, Comm Ave here was Boston's Automobile Row, lined with car dealers.

bucentral.hook: BU legend says if you step on the university seal, you won't graduate in four years.

amory.hook: The B branch is the slowest Green Line branch, with stops only a block or two apart.

babcock.hook: In 1920 the Braves and Brooklyn played 26 innings nearby before darkness ended it in a tie.

packards.hook: Packard's Corner is where Comm Ave bends toward Allston and Brighton.

harvardave.hook: Every September 1, Allston's sidewalks fill with furniture on the city's biggest moving day.

stmarys.hook: In 1889 the first electric streetcar route ran along Beacon Street.

hawes.hook: Hawes Street is one of the quietest stops on the C branch.

kent.hook: Kent Street is a small stop in the middle of Beacon Street.

stpaul.hook: Until 2021 the Green Line had two St. Paul Street stops, one on the B and one on the C.

coolidge.hook: Coolidge Corner is named for an 1857 general store, not the president.

fenway.hook: In 1946 Ted Williams hit a 502-foot home run to the seat now painted red.

prudential.hook: The Prudential Tower (1964) rises 749 feet over old railroad yards.

northeastern.hook: The first modern World Series was played here in 1903, at the Huntington Avenue Grounds.

mfa.hook: The Gardner Museum nearby must stay exactly as Isabella Stewart Gardner arranged it.

broadway.hook: South Boston's St. Patrick's Day parade dates back to 1901.

andrew.hook: Andrew Square is named for John Andrew, the Civil War governor who raised the 54th Massachusetts.

jfk.hook: The John F. Kennedy Presidential Library opened nearby on Columbia Point in 1979.

savin.hook: Savin Hill is named for the savin, a red cedar that once grew on its slopes.

fields.hook: Fields Corner is the heart of Boston's Vietnamese community.

shawmut.hook: Shawmut was the Native name for the peninsula that became Boston.

ashmont.hook: From Ashmont, the Mattapan trolley still runs streetcars built in the 1940s.

nquincy.hook: The Red Line reached Quincy in 1971, when North Quincy opened.

wollaston.hook: Wollaston is named for Captain Richard Wollaston, who settled here in 1625.

quincy.hook: Presidents John Adams and John Quincy Adams are buried in the church across the street.

qadams.hook: The birthplaces of two presidents, John Adams and John Quincy Adams, still stand in Quincy.

braintree.hook: Braintree became the end of the Red Line in 1980.
